Forward Reverse Kernel Regression for the Schrödinger bridge problem

Denis Belomestny1 Address: 1Faculty of Mathematics
Duisburg-Essen University
Thea-Leymann-Str. 9
D-45127 Essen
Germany Email address: denis.belomestny@uni-due.de and John Schoenmakers2 Address: 2Weierstrass Institute for Applied Analysis and Stochastics
Mohrenstr. 39
10117 Berlin
Germany Email address: schoenma@wias-berlin.de
Abstract.

In this paper, we study the Schrödinger Bridge Problem (SBP), which is central to entropic optimal transport. For general reference processes and begin–endpoint distributions, we propose a forward-reverse iterative Monte Carlo procedure to approximate the Schrödinger potentials in a nonparametric way. In particular, we use kernel based Monte Carlo regression in the context of Picard iteration of a corresponding fixed point problem as considered in [5]. By preserving in the iteration positivity and contractivity in a Hilbert metric sense, we develop a provably convergent algorithm. Furthermore, we provide convergence rates for the potential estimates and prove their optimality. Finally, as an application, we propose a non-nested Monte Carlo procedure for the final dimensional distributions of the Schrödinger Bridge process, based on the constructed potentials and the forward-reverse simulation method for conditional diffusions developed in [2].

Key words and phrases:
Schrödinger problem
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
90C40 and 65C05 and 62G08

1. Introduction

The Schrödinger bridge problem (SBP) traces back to a question of Erwin Schrödinger in [24]: among all evolutions of a system that start in a prescribed distribution and end in another one, which is the most likely when likelihood is measured by relative entropy with respect to a fixed reference process ? Besides its physical origin, the SBP is now known as an entropic analogue of optimal transport and as a stochastic control problem [17, 8]. Let the reference Markov process run in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with transition density

q⁡(s,x,t,z),0≤s≤t≤T,x,z∈ℝd.q(s,x;\,t,z),\qquad 0\leq s\leq t\leq T,\;x,z\in\mathbb{R}^{d}.

The aim is to build a Markov process whose joint start-end law

(1) μ⁡(d​x,d​z)=q⁡(0,x,T,z)​ν0​(d​x)​νT​(d​z),\mu(dx,dz)=q(0,x;\,T,z)\,\nu_{0}(dx)\,\nu_{T}(dz),

matches two fixed marginals μ⁡(d​x,ℝd)=ρ0​(x)​d​x,μ⁡(ℝd,d​z)=ρT​(z)​d​z.\mu(dx,\mathbb{R}^{d})=\rho_{0}(x)\,dx,\;\mu(\mathbb{R}^{d},dz)=\rho_{T}(z)\,dz. The unknown measures ν0,νT\nu_{0},\nu_{T} are the boundary potentials. Existence of such potentials was proved by Fortet in one dimension [12], by Beurling in any dimension [4], and revisited through a Banach fixed-point argument in [5]. A recent extension to non-compact supports is given in [11]. Whenever the factorization (1) holds, there exists a Schrödinger Markov process XμX^{\mu} such that for any grid 0<t1<⋯<tn<T0<t_{1}<\dots<t_{n}<T and every bounded Borel function gg on ℝd⁡(n+2)\mathbb{R}^{d(n+2)},

(2) 𝔼⁡[g⁡(X0μ,Xt1μ,…,Xtnμ,XTμ)]=∫ℝd×ℝdμ⁡(𝑑x,𝑑z)​𝔼​[g⁡(x,Xt1x,…,Xtnx,z)|XTx=z]\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[g\bigl(X_{0}^{\mu},X_{t_{1}}^{\mu},\dots,X_{t_{n}}^{\mu},X_{T}^{\mu}\bigr)\bigr]\;=\!\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\mu(dx,dz)\,\mathbb{E}\!\bigl[g\bigl(x,X_{t_{1}}^{x},\dots,X_{t_{n}}^{x},z\bigr)\,\big|\,X_{T}^{x}=z\bigr]

where XxX^{x} denotes the reference process started in xx at time 00. For an arbitrary coupling μ\mu, the right-hand side of (2) still determines a reciprocal process11 1 See Appendix A for a short review., which possesses only a weak (two-time) Markov property. Jamison [14] proved that this process is genuinely Markov if and only if μ\mu factorizes as in (1). In other words, the factorization criterion characterises precisely when a reciprocal family can be promoted to a Markov one - the hallmark of a Schrödinger bridge.

In many presentations of the Schrödinger Bridge problem, one takes a very simple reference process, for instance some Brownian motion with drift, so that its transition kernel is explicitly known, see e.g. [22] and [1]. However, there are several practical and theoretical advantages in considering more general reference processes, for example processes given by multidimensional Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs) possibly restricted to certain domain constraints. Loosely speaking, in the SBP the new process is found by reweighting the paths of the reference process to satisfy the desired endpoint distributions. If the reference is already “close” (in distribution sense) to the target boundary marginals, the amount of correction required is “small”, and iterative numerical procedures may converge rapidly.

In principle, ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} can be computed by a forward–backward iteration scheme analog to the Sinkhorn or IPFP scheme in discrete entropic optimal transport. In particular, if qq is the transition kernel of the reference process and ρ0\rho_{0} and ρT\rho_{T} are prescribed boundary densities, then according to (1), ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} satisfy

ρ0​(x)\displaystyle\rho_{0}(x)\; =ν0​(x)​∫q⁡(0,x,T,z)​νT​(z)​𝑑z,\displaystyle=\;\nu_{0}(x)\,\int q(0,x;T,z)\,\nu_{T}(z)\,dz,
(3) ρT​(z)\displaystyle\rho_{T}(z)\; =νT​(z)​∫q⁡(0,x,T,z)​ν0​(x)​𝑑x,\displaystyle=\;\nu_{T}(z)\,\int q(0,x;T,z)\,\nu_{0}(x)\,dx,

Conceptually, one can attempt a Picard (fixed-point) iteration:

(4) νT(n)⟶ν0(n+1),ν0(n+1)⟶νT(n+1),\nu_{T}^{(n)}\;\longrightarrow\;\nu_{0}^{(n+1)},\quad\nu_{0}^{(n+1)}\;\longrightarrow\;\nu_{T}^{(n+1)},

thus updating each potential function estimate based on an estimate of the other one, until convergence within some prescribed accuracy level is achieved. When the reference process and its transition densities are well understood (e.g., known analytically and low- dimensional), it is possible to discretize and solve these integral equations directly. However, this becomes computationally (too) challenging for more complex reference processes, in particular in higher dimensions.

An attractive alternative is to solve the Schrödinger system (3) stochastically, using Monte Carlo approximations of the involved integrals. More precisely, observe that system (3) can be written in stochastic terms:

(5) ρ0​(x)\displaystyle\rho_{0}(x) =ν0​(x)​𝔼​[νT​(XTx)],\displaystyle\;=\;\nu_{0}(x)\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\nu_{T}(X_{T}^{x})\bigr],
(6) ρT​(z)\displaystyle\rho_{T}(z) =νT​(z)​𝔼​[ν0​(YTz)​𝒴Tz],\displaystyle\;=\;\nu_{T}(z)\,\mathbb{E}\bigl[\,\nu_{0}(Y_{T}^{z})\,\mathcal{Y}_{T}^{z}\bigr],

where XxX^{x} is the “forward” reference process starting in xx at time 00 and (Yz,𝒴z)(Y^{z},\mathcal{Y}^{z}) is a suitably chosen “reverse” process running through ℝd×ℝ+\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}_{+} with (Y0z,𝒴0z)=(z,1)(Y_{0}^{z},\mathcal{Y}_{0}^{z})=(z,1). Let us underline that we do not need to assume an explicit closed-form for the reference transition kernel q⁡(s,x,t,y)q(s,x;t,y). Instead, we only require the ability to sample from the forward process XX with the same dynamics as the reference, and to sample from the “reverse” process (Y,𝒴)(Y,\mathcal{Y}). The construction of the reverse process goes back to [25] for special cases that allow for 𝒴≡1\mathcal{Y}\equiv 1. A generalization to general diffusions was constructed in [19]. The details are spelled out in Appendix B.

Having at hand some estimate νT(n)\nu_{T}^{(n)} say, one may carry out the updates in (4) via the following Monte Carlo kernel regression procedure (rough sketch): We construct

  • •

    forward paths {(X0(i),XT(i))}i=1N\{(X_{0}^{(i)},X_{T}^{(i)})\}_{i=1}^{N} under some initial distribution of X0X_{0},

  • •

    reverse paths {(Y0(j),YT(j),𝒴T(j))}j=1M\{(Y_{0}^{(j)},Y_{T}^{(j)},\mathcal{Y}_{T}^{(j)})\}_{j=1}^{M} under some initial distribution of Y0Y_{0}.

Next, using kernel (Nadaraya–Watson) regression, we approximate the conditional expectation in (5) by

g^​(x)=∑i=1NK⁡((x−X0(i))/δ)​νT(n)​(XT(i))∑i=1NK⁡((x−X0(i))/δ),\widehat{g}(x)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N}K\left((x-X_{0}^{(i)})/\delta\right)\,\nu_{T}^{(n)}(X_{T}^{(i)})}{\sum_{i=1}^{N}K\left((x-X_{0}^{(i)})/\delta\right)},

where KK is a suitable kernel, and set ν0(n+1)​(x)=ρ0​(x)/g^​(x).\nu_{0}^{(n+1)}(x)\;=\;\rho_{0}(x)/\widehat{g}(x). Similarly, we estimate the expectation in (6) by

h^​(x)=∑j=1MK⁡((x−Y0(j))/δ)​ν0(n+1)​(YT(j))​𝒴T(j)∑j=1MK⁡((x−Y0(j))/δ)​𝒴T(j),\widehat{h}(x)\;=\;\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{M}K\left((x-Y_{0}^{(j)})/\delta\right)\,\nu_{0}^{(n+1)}(Y_{T}^{(j)})\mathcal{Y}_{T}^{(j)}}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}K\left((x-Y_{0}^{(j)})/\delta\right)\mathcal{Y}_{T}^{(j)}},

and set νT(n+1)​(x)=ρT​(x)/h^​(x)\nu_{T}^{(n+1)}(x)\;=\;\rho_{T}(x)/\widehat{h}(x).

The above updating procedure may be repeated until no improvement within a certain accuracy level is obtained any more. We thus obtain a continuous approximation to the boundary potentials ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} in a flexible, data-driven manner. In particular, this method provides an explicit functional representation of the Schrödinger boundary potentials in settings where classical deterministic methods are prohibitive, bridging the gap between rigorous entropic optimal transport theory and practical high-dimensional Monte Carlo implementations. Furthermore, we analyze the convergence of the proposed iteration scheme. A cornerstone of our analysis is the fact that the forward–reverse Monte Carlo iteration remains a contraction in the Hilbert projective metric, which is recapitulated in Appendix D. Next as an application we analyze the problem of generating Schrödinger Bridge using hh-transform techniques for SDEs based on the estimated potentials. Finally, as another application, we show that the finite dimensional distributions of a Schrödinger Bridge process can be estimated by a non-nested Monte Carlo procedure if the potentials ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} are given, or constructed by the (likewise non-nested) Monte Carlo procedure presented in this paper. In fact, this is achieved via an application of the forward-reverse simulation procedure for conditional diffusions developed in [2].

Theoretical and numerical analysis of the SBP and its iterative solution has been extensively studied. Léonard [18] provides a foundational overview of the Schrödinger problem, its entropy minimization formulation, and convergence properties. Chen, Georgiou, and Pavon [6] interpret the SBP in terms of stochastic control and analyze the convergence of the iterative scaling algorithm. Peyré and Cuturi [21] frame the problem within entropic optimal transport and demonstrate numerical schemes based on Sinkhorn iteration. Benamou et al. [3] introduce iterative Bregman projections, a generalization of Picard iteration for entropy-regularized problems. Cominetti, Soto, and Ríos [7] analyze the convergence rate of Sinkhorn-like iterations. De Bortoli et al. [9] explore neural approaches that learn Schrödinger potentials using iterative schemes as part of model training. Pavon, Tabak, and Trigila [20] propose an iterative method for solving the Schrödinger bridge problem when the marginals are only known via samples. Their approach generalizes Fortet–Sinkhorn iterations by combining importance sampling and constrained maximum likelihood estimation to propagate the Schrödinger potentials. This sample-based method is particularly well-suited for high-dimensional applications, where grid-based methods become infeasible.

In contrast to classical approaches relying on analytic forms of the transition density of the reference process [18, 6, 3], our paper offers a nonparametric and data-driven framework in the case of general reference processes for which only a generative model is available. We develop a kernel-based estimation methodology that allows for efficient estimation of Schrödinger potentials using forward and reverse samples from the reference process. Furthermore, we establish strong theoretical guarantees for the convergence and performance of the proposed method. Notably, we derive for the first time in the literature minimax-optimal rates of functional approximation for the Schrödinger potentials in Hilbert’s metric based on samples from the reference process.

The paper is organized as follows. First, we review the Schrödinger Bridge problem and introduce some notations in Section 2. Section 3 is devoted to the description of our iterative kernel regression algorithm. In Section 4, we present our convergence analysis. A short perturbation analysis of the actual trajectories of the SB due to approximated potentials is done in Section 5. In Section 6 we outline a non-nested simulation procedure for the finite dimensional distributions of a Schrödinger Bridge process. The proofs of our convergence results are deferred to Section 7. Appendices A–F recapitulate the for our goals relevant concepts and results from the literature.

2. Schrödinger problem as a fixed point problem

In this section, we present the essentials of the Schrödinger system (1) following [5].

Theorem 1.

[5, Prop. 1] Let q⁡(0,⋅,T,⋅)q(0,\cdot;T,\cdot) be continuous and strictly positive on ℝd×ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}. Then for given densities ρ0\rho_{0} and ρT\rho_{T} with compact supports 𝖲0⊂ℝd\mathsf{S}_{0}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and 𝖲T⊂ℝd,\mathsf{S}_{T}\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, respectively, there exist Borel measurable functions ν0:𝖲0→ℝ≥0\nu_{0}:\mathsf{S}_{0}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} and νT:𝖲T→ℝ≥0\nu_{T}:\mathsf{S}_{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} such that

ρ0​(x)\displaystyle\rho_{0}(x) =ν0(x)∫𝖲Tq(0,x;T,z)νT(z)dz, a.e. on 𝖲0,\displaystyle=\nu_{0}(x)\int_{\mathsf{S}_{T}}q(0,x;T,z)\nu_{T}(z)\,dz,\text{ a.e. on }\mathsf{S}_{0},
(7) ρT​(z)\displaystyle\rho_{T}(z) =νT(z)∫𝖲0q(0,x;T,z)ν0(x)dx a.e. on 𝖲T.\displaystyle=\nu_{T}(z)\int_{\mathsf{S}_{0}}q(0,x;T,z)\nu_{0}(x)\,dx\text{ a.e. on }\mathsf{S}_{T}.

Moreover, if ν0′\nu_{0}^{\prime} and νT′\nu_{T}^{\prime} is another pair of solutions, one has that ν0′=c​ν0\nu_{0}^{\prime}=c\nu_{0} and νT′=c−1​νT\nu_{T}^{\prime}=c^{-1}\nu_{T} for some c>0.c>0.

Corollary 2.

If ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} are as in Theorem 1, then there is a reciprocal Markov process XμX^{\mu} with finite dimensional distributions (2), where μ⁡(d​x,d​z)=q⁡(0,x,T,z)​ν0​(x)​νT​(z)​d​x​d​z.\mu\left(dx,dz\right)=q(0,x;T,z)\nu_{0}(x)\nu_{T}(z)\,dx\,dz.

Theorem 1 can be proved by establishing the contraction of an operator 𝒞\mathcal{C} defined as

(8) 𝒞[g]=∫𝖲0ρ0​(x)∫𝖲Tq⁡(0,x,T,z)​ρT​(z)g⁡(z)​𝑑zq(0,x;T,⋅)dx\mathcal{C}[g]=\int_{\mathsf{S}_{0}}\frac{\rho_{0}(x)}{\int_{\mathsf{S}_{T}}q(0,x;T,z)\frac{\rho_{T}(z)}{g(z)}\,dz}q(0,x;T,\cdot)\,dx

in the Hilbert metric (Appendix D). The operator 𝒞⁡[g]\mathcal{C}[g] is essentially a composition of positive linear integral transforms (with strictly positive kernels) and pointwise reciprocals of functions. These operations preserve positivity, so 𝒞⁡[g]\mathcal{C}[g] remains strictly positive whenever gg is. Moreover, 𝒞\mathcal{C} is positively homogeneous, meaning that scaling gg by a positive constant does not affect the “core” of the map. This is precisely why the Hilbert distance dH​(f,g)d_{H}(f,g) between two strictly positive functions ff and gg is the natural choice here: it is invariant under scalings of ff and gg with arbitrary positive scaling factors (for further details see Appendix D). Then Birkhoff’s theorem essentially implies that such compositions of strictly positive integral operators and reciprocal maps become strict contractions in the Hilbert metric on the cone

ℒ+∞(𝖲T):=⋃ε>0ℒε∞(𝖲T) with ℒε∞(𝖲T):={f∈ℒ∞(𝖲T):f(x)≥ε for a.e. x∈𝖲T}\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}):={\displaystyle\bigcup\limits_{\varepsilon>0}}\mathcal{L}_{\varepsilon}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T})\text{ with }\mathcal{L}_{\varepsilon}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}):=\left\{f\in\mathcal{L}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}):f(x)\geq\varepsilon\text{ \ for a.e. }x\in\mathsf{S}_{T}\right\}

under suitable irreducibility assumptions. For details and a historical overview see [16] for example. In [5] it is shown that for 𝒞\mathcal{C} given by (8), under the conditions of Theorem 1, there is a constant κ=κ⁡(𝒞)<1\kappa=\kappa(\mathcal{C})<1 such that

dH​(𝒞⁡[f],𝒞⁡[g])≤κ​dH​(f,g),d_{H}(\mathcal{C}[f],\mathcal{C}[g])\,\leq\,\kappa\,d_{H}(f,g),

for all strictly positive f,gf,g ∈\in ℒ+∞​(𝖲T)\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}). So by the usual fixed-point argument (adapted to the metric dHd_{H} that ignores scalar multiples), 𝒞\mathcal{C} has a unique fixed point (up to scaling) that satisfies 𝒞⁡(g⋆)=g⋆\mathcal{C}\left(g^{\star}\right)=g^{\star} in dHd_{H} sense, that is 𝒞⁡(g⋆)=α​g⋆\mathcal{C}\left(g^{\star}\right)=\alpha g^{\star} almost everywhere for some α>0.\alpha>0. In [5] it is moreover shown that α=1\alpha=1, and that g⋆g^{\star} is continuous, i.e. has a version in ℒ+∞​(𝖲T)\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}) that is continuous on the whole 𝖲T\mathsf{S}_{T}. Then given this g⋆g^{\star} satisfying 𝒞⁡(g⋆)=g⋆\mathcal{C}\left(g^{\star}\right)=g^{\star} almost everywhere, the solution in Theorem 1 is obviously determined by

    If both start and end point distribution are degenerated, we thus have the classical bridge and get νT=cδ(⋅−z0)\nu_{T}=c\delta(\cdot-z_{0}) and ν0=c−1q(0,x0,1,z0)−1δ(⋅−x0),\nu_{0}=c^{-1}q(0,x_{0},1,z_{0})^{-1}\delta(\cdot-x_{0}), where c>0c>0 can be taken arbitrarily.

So, in the above degenerate cases the Schrödinger problem has a relatively trivial solution. We henceforth assume that both start and end point distribution are non-degenerated.

3. Iterative approximation procedure

In this section we will spell out in detail an iterative Monte Carlo regression procedure as heuristically sketched in Section 1. The procedure yields an approximation to the fixed point g⋆g^{\star} of the operator (8), and hence via (9) an approximation to the potential functions ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} due to Theorem 1. The operator (8) may be decomposed as

(10) 𝒞=ℰ0∘𝒟0∘ℰT∘𝒟T\mathcal{C}=\mathcal{E}_{0}\circ\mathcal{D}_{0}\circ\mathcal{E}_{T}\circ\mathcal{D}_{T}

with

𝒟0\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{0} :ℒ+∞​(𝖲0)∋f→1/f∈ℒ+∞​(𝖲0),\displaystyle:\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{0})\ni f\rightarrow 1/f\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{0}),
𝒟T\displaystyle\mathcal{D}_{T} :ℒ+∞​(𝖲T)∋f→1/f∈ℒ+∞​(𝖲T),\displaystyle:\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T})\ni f\rightarrow 1/f\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}),
ℰT\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{T} :ℒ+∞​(𝖲T)∋f→∫𝖲Tq⁡(0,⋅,T,z)​ρT​(z)​f​(z)​𝑑z∈ℒ+∞​(𝖲0),\displaystyle:\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T})\ni f\rightarrow\int_{\mathsf{S}_{T}}q(0,\cdot;T,z)\rho_{T}(z)f(z)\,dz\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{0}),
ℰ0\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{0} :ℒ+∞(𝖲0)∋f→∫𝖲0ρ0(x)f(x)q(0,x;T,⋅)dx∈ℒ+∞(𝖲T).\displaystyle:\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{0})\ni f\rightarrow\int_{\mathsf{S}_{0}}\rho_{0}(x)f(x)q(0,x;T,\cdot)\,dx\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}).

The operators ℰ0\mathcal{E}_{0} and ℰT\mathcal{E}_{T} have, respectively, the following stochastic representations

ℰT​[f]​(x)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{T}[f](x) =𝔼[ρT(XTx)f(XTx)], f∈ℒ+∞(𝖲T),\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\rho_{T}(X_{T}^{x})f(X_{T}^{x})\right],\text{ \ \ }f\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{T}),
ℰ0​[f]​(z)\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{0}[f](z) =𝔼[ρ0(YTz)f(YTz)𝒴Tz], f∈ℒ+∞(𝖲0)\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}\left[\rho_{0}(Y_{T}^{z})f(Y_{T}^{z})\mathcal{Y}_{T}^{z}\right],\text{ \ \ }f\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}_{0})

where (Y,𝒴)(Y,\mathcal{Y}) is termed a reverse process, see Appendix B for more details and references on reverse processes in diffusion setting.

Remark 3 (Reverse diffusion vs. time-reversed diffusion).

It should be noted that the term “reverse” diffusion for YY is somewhat misleading as it differs from the time-reversed diffusion in the sense of Haussmann and Pardoux [13]. For specifying the dynamics of the latter one explicitly needs the transition density of XX. In contrast, the SDE dynamics of YY is straightforwardly inferred from the SDE dynamics of XX and has usually similar regularity properties. A key advantage of our “reverse” diffusion is that it can be constructed far more simply than the time-reversed diffusion in [13]. As a consequence, integrals of the form ∫g(x)q(0,x,T,⋅)dx\int g(x)\,q(0,x,T,\cdot)\,dx can be computed by simulation of “reverse” stochastic representations involving YY, more simply than by representations relying on the real “time-reversed” diffusion. Although the term “reverse” might thus be considered kind of a misnomer, it is nonetheless maintained in this paper because it stems from our main background references [2] and [19].

In the sequel, we make the following assumptions.

Assumption 4.

Let the transition density qq, the densities ρ0,\rho_{0}, ρT\rho_{T} and their respective supports 𝖲0,\mathsf{S}_{0}, 𝖲T\mathsf{S}_{T} be as in Theorem 1. If one only needs some expected functionals of the SB depending on its finite dimensional distributions, we propose a more efficient way of estimation in the next section.

6. Forward-Reverse simulation for reciprocal and Schrödinger processes

In Appendix A we have recapitulated the concept of reciprocal processes in general and Schrödinger processes in particular, being reciprocal Markov process with endpoint distribution satisfying (1). In this section we propose simulation based approaches for estimating functionals of the form (31), hence the finite dimensional distributions of such processes. The here proposed methods may be seen as an application of the forward-reverse approach developed in [2], recapitulated in Appendices B-C, combined with the simulation based construction of the Schrödinger measures or potentials developed in Section 3.

6.1. Stochastic representations for reciprocal processes

By combining (31) (see also (32)) with (39) we immediately obtain an FR stochastic representation for the finite dimensional distributions of a reciprocal process due to a begin-endpoint measure μ⁡(d​x,d​z)\mu(dx,dz):

Due to the FR simulation procedure for the representation (39), a straightforward simulation procedure for (21) suggests itself: One may sample a number of pairs (X0(r),ZT(r)),(X_{0}^{(r)},Z_{T}^{(r)}), r=1,…,R,r=1,\ldots,R, from the distribution μ.\mu. One finally takes the average over RR estimations in order to obtain an estimate of (21). Obviously, this nested simulation procedure will be generally slow as it requires the simulation of order N​RNR trajectories. In the next section we propose a more efficient (non-nested) Monte Carlo procedure for computing (21) in the case of a Schrödinger process.

6.2. Stochastic representations for Schrödinger processes

A Schrödinger Markov process is determined by a begin-endpoint distribution μ\mu of the form (1) due to σ\sigma-finite Borel measures ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} satisfying

∫ℝd×ℝdν0​(𝑑x)​q​(0,x,T,z)​νT​(𝑑z)=1.\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\nu_{0}(dx)q(0,x,T,z)\nu_{T}(dz)=1.

Conversely, any pair of Borel measures ν~0\widetilde{\nu}_{0} and ν~T\widetilde{\nu}_{T} on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with

(22) 0<c0,T−1:=∫ℝd×ℝdν~0​(𝑑x)​q​(0,x,T,z)​ν~T​(𝑑z)<∞0<c_{0,T}^{-1}:=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}}\widetilde{\nu}_{0}(dx)q(0,x,T,z)\widetilde{\nu}_{T}(dz)<\infty

gives rise to a begin-endpoint distribution of the form (1) due to

(23) μ⁡(d​x,d​z)\displaystyle\mu(dx,dz) =c0,T​ν~0​(d​x)​q​(0,x,T,z)​ν~T​(d​z)\displaystyle=c_{0,T}\widetilde{\nu}_{0}(dx)q(0,x,T,z)\widetilde{\nu}_{T}(dz)

with ν0=c0,T1/2​ν~0\nu_{0}=c_{0,T}^{1/2}\widetilde{\nu}_{0} and νT=c0,T1/2​ν~T.\nu_{T}=c_{0,T}^{1/2}\widetilde{\nu}_{T}. Obviously, if μ\mu is defined via (22) and (23) for given ν~0\widetilde{\nu}_{0} or ν~T,\widetilde{\nu}_{T}, it is invariant under scaling of ν~0\widetilde{\nu}_{0} or ν~T\widetilde{\nu}_{T} by an arbitrary positive constant. Thus if, moreover, ν~0\widetilde{\nu}_{0} or ν~T\widetilde{\nu}_{T} is a finite measure, we may w.l.o.g. assume that it is a probability measures.

We now assume that, either, we are given a pair of probability measures ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} that define an endpoint distribution μ\mu in (1), or we are given μ\mu and assume that ν0\nu_{0} and νT\nu_{T} are obtained via the approximation procedure of Section 3.

Remark 9.

Note that one has that

𝔼⁡[ζε​(g⁡(x,⋅,z),Xx,Yz,𝒴z,x,z)]≲q⁡(0,x,T,z),\mathbb{E}\left[\zeta_{\varepsilon}(g\left(x,\cdot,z\right);X^{x},Y^{z},\mathcal{Y}^{z};x,z)\right]\lesssim q(0,x,T,z),

where the right-hand-side is integrable with respect to ν~0⊗ν~T\widetilde{\nu}_{0}\otimes\widetilde{\nu}_{T} due to assumption (22). In the case where ν~0\widetilde{\nu}_{0} or ν~T\widetilde{\nu}_{T} is not a finite measure one then may design a similar FR simulation procedure based on some importance sampling or MCMC technique. We omit the details.

Remark 10.

The estimator (26) due to a generic test functional gg allows for estimating the probability that the Schrödinger Bridge process XμX^{\mu} (see (20)) visits at arbitrarily chosen discrete times arbitrarily chosen (Borel) regions. We underline that this estimator acts on trajectories generated by the reference process XX and its corresponding reverse process YY only, and thus simulation of the actual trajectories of the SB process XμX^{\mu} is not needed for this purpose. Furthermore, in the previous section it is shown that simulation of the real trajectories of XμX^{\mu} via (20) may be a delicate issue, particularly in cases where νT\nu_{T} is approximated and time tt approaches the terminal time TT. Moreover, in (20) one needs to compute hh at any time 0≤t≤T,0\leq t\leq T, which either requires knowledge of the transition density qq or requires extra sub-simulations at each simulated trajectory. Further one could say that simulation of (20) is related to simulation of conditional diffusion trajectories (e.g. see[23]), which is known to be a delicate issue for similar reasons.

    𝔼[(H^εN,N,N(g;x,y)−H(g;x,y))2]=𝒪(N−8/(4+d))\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\widehat{H}_{\varepsilon_{N},N,N}(g;x,y)-H(g;x,y)\right)^{2}\right]=\mathcal{O}(N^{-8/(4+d)}).

Hence, in particular, for a second order kernel KK and d≤4d\leq 4, both H⁡(g,x,y)H(g;x,y) and H⁡(1,x,y)=q⁡(0,x,T,y)H(1;x,y)=q(0,x,T,y) in (39) may be approximated with 1/N1/\sqrt{N} accuracy by using NN forward trajectories of XX and NN “reverse” trajectories of (Y,𝒴)(Y,\mathcal{Y}). One so may obtain an estimate for ℰ⁡(g)\mathcal{E}(g) by the ratio of these respective approximations.

Appendix D Hilbert metric

Let ℒ+∞​(𝖲)\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}) denote the set of (equivalence classes of) strictly positive measurable functions on 𝖲\mathsf{S} that are essentially bounded away from zero. For two such functions f,g∈ℒ+∞​(𝖲)f,g\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}), define

M⁡(f,g)\displaystyle M(f,g) :⁣=\displaystyle:= inf{λ>0:f≤λ​g​ a.e.},\displaystyle\inf\{\lambda>0:f\leq\lambda\,g\text{ a.e.}\},
m⁡(f,g)\displaystyle m(f,g) :⁣=\displaystyle:= sup{λ>0:λ​g≤f​ a.e.},\displaystyle\sup\{\lambda>0:\lambda\,g\leq f\text{ a.e.}\},

and

dH​(f,g):=log⁡(M⁡(f,g)m⁡(f,g))\displaystyle d_{H}(f,g):=\log\Bigl(\tfrac{M(f,g)}{m(f,g)}\Bigr)

with inf∅=+∞,\inf\varnothing=+\infty, by definition. If m⁡(f,g)=0m(f,g)=0 or M⁡(f,g)=+∞M(f,g)=+\infty, then by convention dH​(f,g)=+∞d_{H}(f,g)=+\infty. Moreover, since dH​(α​f,α​g)=dH​(f,g)d_{H}(\alpha f,\alpha g)=d_{H}(f,g) for any α>0\alpha>0, one regards dHd_{H} as a metric on the equivalence classes of functions generated by the relation

f∼g⟺fg≡constant a.e.f\,\sim\,g\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\frac{f}{g}\equiv\text{constant a.e.}

Equivalently, dH​(f,g)=0d_{H}(f,g)=0 if and only if f∼gf\sim g.

Lemma 13.

For f,g∈ℒ+∞​(𝖲)f,g\in\mathcal{L}_{+}^{\infty}(\mathsf{S}) one has that

one has

=suplog⁡(f/g)+suplog⁡(g/f)\displaystyle=\sup\log\left(f/g\right)+\sup\log\left(g/f\right)

dH​(f,g)≤2​‖log⁡f−log⁡g‖∞.d_{H}(f,g)\leq 2\left\|\log f-\log g\right\|_{\infty}.

since ‖f−g‖∞≤‖g‖∞​(sup(f/g)−1).\|f-g\|_{\infty}\leq\|g\|_{\infty}(\sup(f/g)-1). For the case 1≤sup(f/g)≤sup(g/f)1\leq\sup(f/g)\leq\sup(g/f) we may exchange ff and gg in (41), and we are done. ∎

If f⁡(x+)−g⁡(x+)>0f(x_{+})-g(x_{+})>0 and f⁡(x−)−g⁡(x−)<0f(x_{-})-g(x_{-})<0 there exists x0∈𝖲x_{0}\in\mathsf{S} with f⁡(x0)−g⁡(x0)=0f(x_{0})-g(x_{0})=0 since 𝖲\mathsf{S} is connected, hence f⁡(x0)/g⁡(x0)=1.f(x_{0})/g(x_{0})=1. ∎

Appendix E Smoothness classes and Hölder spaces

In this section we recall some classical terminology on smoothness classifications from standard analysis. For an open domain U⊂ℝdU\subset\mathbb{R}^{d}, the space Ck​(U)C^{k}(U), k∈ℕ0,k\in\mathbb{N}_{0}, denotes the space of functions f:U→ℝf:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R} that have continuous partial derivatives up to order kk. Formally, these derivatives are described by a differential operator D𝜸D^{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}} of order |𝜸|,\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|, where 𝜸=(γ1,…,γd)∈ℕ0d{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}=(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{d})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d} is a multi-index, |𝜸|=∑i=1dγi,\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\gamma_{i}, and

D𝜸f:=∂|𝜸|f∂x1γ1⋯∂xdγd, for f∈Ck(U).D^{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}f:=\frac{\partial^{|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}|}f}{\partial x_{1}^{\gamma_{1}}\cdots\partial x_{d}^{\gamma_{d}}},\text{ \ for \ \ }f\in C^{k}(U).

For clarity, multi-indices are distinguished by using bold font. If UU is bounded, we denote by Ck​(U¯)C^{k}(\overline{U}) the space of uniformly continuous functions f:U→ℝf:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R} with uniformly continuous partial derivatives up to order kk. Hence, if f∈Ck​(U¯)f\in C^{k}(\overline{U}) then ff and all his partial derivatives extend to continuous functions on U¯.\overline{U}.

A function f:U→ℝf:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is said to be uniformly α\alpha-Hölder continuous with exponent α\alpha for some 0<α≤10<\alpha\leq 1, if

[f]α,U:=supx≠y∈U|f⁡(x)−f⁡(y)||x−y|α<∞[f]_{\alpha,U}:=\sup_{x\neq y\in U}\frac{|f(x)-f(y)|}{|x-y|^{\alpha}}<\infty

with |⋅|\left|\cdot\right| being a particularly chosen norm on ℝd.\mathbb{R}^{d}. The function ff is said to be locally uniformly α\alpha-Hölder continuous, if [f]α,U′<∞[f]_{\alpha,U^{\prime}}<\infty for any bounded open set U′U^{\prime} with U′¯⊂U,\overline{U^{\prime}}\subset U, i.e. for any open set U′U^{\prime} that is compactly contained in U.U. The space of locally uniformly α\alpha-Hölder continuous functions in UU is denoted by ℋ0,α​(U).\mathcal{H}^{0,\alpha}(U). If UU is bounded, we denote by ℋ0,α​(U¯)\mathcal{H}^{0,\alpha}(\overline{U}) the space of uniformly α\alpha-Hölder continuous functions in U.U. Note that any uniformly α\alpha-Hölder continuous functions in UU extends to an α\alpha-Hölder continuous function in U¯.\overline{U}.

We next define for an open domain U⊂ℝdU\subset\mathbb{R}^{d} and k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0} the space

ℋk,α(U):={f:U→ℝ:f∈Ck(U) and D𝜸f∈ℋ0,α(U) for all 𝜸 with |𝜸|=k},\mathcal{H}^{k,\alpha}(U):=\left\{f:U\rightarrow\mathbb{R}:f\in C^{k}(U)\text{ and }D^{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}f\in\mathcal{H}^{0,\alpha}(U)\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\text{ with }\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|=k\right\},

and for open and bounded U,U, the space ℋk,α​(U¯)\mathcal{H}^{k,\alpha}(\overline{U}) is defined as

ℋk,α(U¯):={f:Ω→ℝ:f∈Ck(U¯) and D𝜸f∈ℋ0,α(U¯) for all 𝜸 with |𝜸|=k}.\mathcal{H}^{k,\alpha}(\overline{U}):=\left\{f:\Omega\rightarrow\mathbb{R}:f\in C^{k}(\overline{U})\text{ and }D^{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}f\in\mathcal{H}^{0,\alpha}(\overline{U})\text{ for all }{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\text{ with }\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|=k\right\}.

It is well known that ℋk,α​(U¯)\mathcal{H}^{k,\alpha}(\overline{U}) is a Banach space with norm

‖f‖ℋk,α​(U¯)=max⁡(max|𝜸|≤k⁡‖D𝜸​f‖∞,U,max|𝜸|=k⁡[D𝜸​f]α,U).\|f\|_{\mathcal{H}^{k,\alpha}(\overline{U})}=\max\left(\max_{\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|\leq k}\left\|D^{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}f\right\|_{\infty,U},\max_{\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|=k}[D^{{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}}f]_{\alpha,U}\right).
Remark 17.

(i) For open and bounded U,U, let f∈ℋk,α​(U¯)f\in\mathcal{H}^{k,\alpha}(\overline{U}) for some fixed k∈ℕ0k\in\mathbb{N}_{0} and 0<α≤1.0<\alpha\leq 1. One then has for all 𝜸{\boldsymbol{\gamma}} with |𝜸|≤k\left|{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\right|\leq k and all x,y∈U,x,y\in U,

Let (X,Y),(X1,Y1),(X2,Y2),…(X,Y),(X_{1},Y_{1}),(X_{2},Y_{2}),\dots be independent random vectors in ℝd×ℝ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{R} with joint density fX​Yf_{XY} and marginal density defined by

In particular, for any fixed φ\varphi the estimate rn,φr_{n,\varphi} converges to

rφ​(x):=∫φ⁡(y)​fX​Y​(x,y)​𝑑yr_{\varphi}(x):=\int\varphi(y)f_{XY}(x,y)dy

under suitable conditions that are given below.

We now turn to the stochastic part of the error. The next result can be extracted from Section 3 of [10].

Theorem 18.

Let Φ\Phi be a VC-type class of functions with envelope function F⁡(y):=supφ∈Φφ⁡(y).F(y):=\sup_{\varphi\in\Phi}\varphi(y). Suppose that

μ2=supx∈𝖲𝔼⁡[F2​(Y)|X=x]<∞.\mu_{2}=\sup_{x\in\mathsf{S}}\mathbb{E}\left[F^{2}(Y)|X=x\right]<\infty.

Then it holds

𝔼⁡[supφ∈Φ‖rn,φ−𝔼⁡[rn,φ]‖𝖲]≤Cδd​n​𝔼⁡[(G⁡(X,Y))2]\mathbb{E}\Bigl[\sup_{\varphi\in\Phi}\left\|r_{n,\varphi}-\mathbb{E}[r_{n,\varphi}]\right\|_{\mathsf{S}}\Bigr]\leq\frac{C}{\delta^{d}\sqrt{n}}\sqrt{\mathbb{E}\left[\left(G(X,Y)\right)^{2}\right]}

with G⁡(x,y)=supφ∈Φsupz∈𝖲gφ,z​(x,y)G(x,y)=\sup_{\varphi\in\Phi}\sup_{z\in\mathsf{S}}g_{\varphi,z}(x,y) and some constant C>0C>0 where gφ,z​(x,y)=φ⁡(y)​K​((z−x)/δ).g_{\varphi,z}(x,y)=\varphi(y)K((z-x)/\delta).

Corollary 19.

Note that it holds

≤δd​κ2​∫−∞∞𝔼⁡[F2​(Y)∣X=z−u​δ]​fX​(z−u​h)​𝑑u\displaystyle\leq\delta^{d}\kappa^{2}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\mathbb{E}\left[F^{2}(Y)\mid X=z-u\delta\right]f_{X}(z-uh)\,du
≤δd​κ2​‖fX‖𝖲​μ2.\displaystyle\leq\delta^{d}\kappa^{2}\|f_{X}\|_{\mathsf{S}}\mu_{2}.

Hence
